text: The man in red smiles up at you from the front page.
You pick it up. The paper is soft and yellow, like it's been lying there for years.
The date under the headline is nineteen eighty seven. November third.
You look down the car. Every newspaper has the same date.
June doesn't look up from her knitting. "Put it down, sweetheart."
"Where did he go?" you ask.
June's needles stop. Her eyes go to the door at the end of the car.
Through its little window, the last car is dark. One handle swings back and forth.
"He's not in there," June says. "Not anymore."
Then, from the last car, a phone starts ringing.
His ringtone. It rings and rings. Nobody turns a page.
Without meaning to, you start to stand.
June's hand clamps onto your knee. "Never the last car. Never."
The ringing stops.
Above you, the lights flicker.
June squeezes your hand. "Eyes shut, sweetheart. Now."
The lights go out. You squeeze your eyes shut.
In the dark, only the clack of the tracks.
Then, from the end of the car: click.
Click. Closer.
Click. Right beside your ear.
You can feel someone bending over you, waiting for you to look.
You don't look.
The doors chime.
The lights are back. June lets out a long breath. "Good. That was good."
Then you notice the passengers.
For the first time, every one of them has turned a page.
In your pocket, your phone buzzes.
Still no signal. But someone is calling.
It's your mom.
June goes very still. "Don't, sweetheart."
But it's your mom. Your thumb is already on the green button.
"Mom?"
Nothing. Then, very softly, in her voice, it says your name.
"I'm waiting at the next stop. Get off the train."
